overview: Allosaurus fragilis was the dominant predator of the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation, reaching nearly ten metres and 2.7 tonnes. Its wide-opening jaws were used in a distinctive axe-strike attack — driving the upper jaw downward into prey — rather than the crushing bite of a tyrannosaur, allowing it to wound and incapacitate animals far larger than itself.

Dozens of specimens are known, making it one of the best-studied large theropods. The Cleveland-Lloyd Quarry in Utah has yielded over 70 individuals — probably a predator trap accumulation. Direct fossil evidence of predator-prey interaction with Stegosaurus survives as reciprocal bone injuries on both species.

articles.title: Discovery
articles.body: Named by Marsh in 1877 from fragmentary material, Allosaurus became properly known through numerous Morrison Formation quarries. "Big Al" — a 95% complete juvenile from Wyoming (1991) — and "Big Al Two" (2002) provided exceptional anatomical and pathological detail. A. jimmadseni (named 2020) is now recognised as a slightly older, distinct species from earlier Morrison strata.

articles.title: Feeding mechanics
articles.body: Biomechanical analysis shows relatively low bite force for its size but an extremely wide gape (up to 79°). The axe-strike hypothesis — driving the upper jaw into prey like a hatchet — is supported by skull kinetics studies. Three large curved hand claws gripped prey during the strike. An Allosaurus vertebra pierced by a Stegosaurus tail spike, and Stegosaurus plates bearing Allosaurus tooth marks, are the most direct evidence of predator-prey interaction in the Morrison.

articles.title: Population biology
articles.body: Growth ring analysis shows adult size was reached in 15–20 years, with mortality peaking at intermediate juvenile stages. The Cleveland-Lloyd concentration — animals attracted to mired prey over years — implies Allosaurus was at times an opportunistic scavenger as well as an active hunter. It was sympatric with Ceratosaurus and the rarer Torvosaurus, likely occupying distinct prey-size niches.

record.description: Allosaurus was a large allosaurid theropod abundant in the Morrison Formation of western North America. Many skulls and skeletons document its anatomy and growth, although the boundaries and diagnoses of named species remain under active revision.
facts: A. fragilis and A. jimmadseni are widely recognised North American species.
Bonebeds and healed injuries provide population-level evidence but do not establish pack hunting or a single feeding strategy.

animalParagraphs: Allosaurus was a large, two-legged meat-eater that lived across the floodplains of western North America in the Late Jurassic. Typical adults were about eight to nine metres long and weighed roughly one and a half to two tonnes; a few individuals were larger, and the upper end of its size range is still debated because the biggest bones are fragmentary or of contested identity.

Its skull was lightweight for its size, with a pair of short horn-like bosses in front of the eyes and rows of serrated, blade-like teeth. The neck was strongly muscled, the arms were relatively long with three large hooked claws, and the tail was long and deep. Biomechanical work suggests the jaws opened very widely and that the skull was built to withstand vertical strikes rather than an exceptionally powerful bite.

Two species are widely recognised from the Morrison Formation: Allosaurus fragilis and the somewhat older A. jimmadseni, named in 2020. Because the genus is known from so many individuals of different sizes, it is a standard reference for theropod growth, injury and skull function. Bonebeds such as the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry preserve dozens of animals together, but how they came to be there, and whether Allosaurus ever cooperated when feeding, remains unresolved.
animalHighlights: A light, deep skull with short paired brow bosses and serrated blade-like teeth, capable of a very wide gape.
Long, powerful arms with three strongly curved claws, unlike the reduced forelimbs of later tyrannosaurs.
Dozens of individuals from juveniles to large adults, including one of the most complete theropod skeletons known.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: Blade-like teeth, tooth-marked bones of Morrison sauropods and stegosaurs, and a puncture in an Allosaurus tail vertebra matching a Stegosaurus tail spike record predation and combat. Cooperative hunting is not established.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Hindlimb anatomy and Morrison trackways support two-legged walking; running speed estimates rest on biomechanical models rather than direct observation.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Several near-complete skeletons fix the size of ordinary adults; the largest reported individuals rest on isolated bones whose species identity is contested.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Proportions are known from complete skeletons. No skin impressions, feathers, colour or the exact form of the brow horns' keratin covering are directly preserved.

presentation.classificationSummary: Allosaurus is the name-bearing genus of Allosauridae within Allosauroidea, a group of large tetanuran theropods. Its position is stable; the live questions concern how many species the Morrison material contains and whether the giant Saurophaganax bones belong to Allosaurus.

questions.title: How many species are there?
questions.copy: Allosaurus fragilis and A. jimmadseni are widely accepted. Older names such as A. europaeus, Antrodemus and Creosaurus, and the referral of individual specimens, still need specimen-by-specimen treatment.

questions.title: Did it hunt in groups?
questions.copy: Bonebeds with many individuals have been read as evidence of gregarious behaviour, but they can equally represent predator traps or repeated attraction to carcasses. No direct evidence of cooperative hunting exists.

questions.title: How big did it get?
questions.copy: Ordinary adults are well measured, but the largest bones assigned to Allosaurus or to Saurophaganax are isolated, so the maximum size and its taxonomic meaning remain open.

specimens.name: Holotype of Allosaurus fragilis
specimens.note: Fragmentary: a partial tooth, a few vertebral centra, rib fragments and a toe bone from Garden Park, Colorado, described by Marsh in 1877. Too incomplete to diagnose the species on its own; USNM 4734 has been proposed as a neotype.

specimens.name: Holotype of Allosaurus jimmadseni
specimens.note: A nearly complete, largely articulated skeleton with skull from the Salt Wash Member at Dinosaur National Monument, Utah, described by Chure and Loewen in 2020.

specimens.name: "Big Al"
specimens.note: A subadult skeleton from the Howe Quarry area, Wyoming, about 95 per cent complete with numerous healed and unhealed injuries; now generally referred to A. jimmadseni.

specimens.name: Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry assemblage
specimens.note: Thousands of disarticulated bones representing at least 46 Allosaurus individuals of all sizes, the basis of Madsen's 1976 osteology.

panel.headline: Dozens of skulls and skeletons from the Morrison Formation, several nearly complete.
panel.standfirst: Allosaurus is one of the best-sampled large theropods. Near-complete articulated skeletons, complete skulls and a bonebed holding at least 46 individuals document every part of the body across a wide range of ages. The weak point is the name itself: the original holotype is a handful of fragments.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Every skeletal region is known from multiple individuals, including articulated skulls, complete limbs and a growth series from juveniles to large adults.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Complete skulls with dentition and braincases, full vertebral columns, pectoral and pelvic girdles, forelimbs with three-clawed hands, hindlimbs and feet, furculae and gastralia, from many individuals. Pathologies such as healed fractures and infections are common, and bone histology has been sampled across the growth series.
knownRemains.note: The Marsh holotype YPM 1930 is too fragmentary to diagnose the species, so the identity of Allosaurus fragilis rests in practice on well-preserved referred skeletons and a proposed neotype rather than on the name-bearing specimen.

media.title: Casts of the holotype YPM 1930, figured by Gilmore in 1920
media.alt: Photographic plate from 1920 showing a toe bone and two vertebral centra of the Allosaurus fragilis holotype
media.caption: Gilmore's 1920 plate of casts of the type specimen: a proximal toe phalanx, a posterior dorsal centrum and a probable sacral centrum. It shows how little of the name-bearing animal exists compared with the referred skeletons.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Many complete skulls with teeth, palates, braincases and hyoids, including the articulated skull of the A. jimmadseni holotype.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Complete cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal series in several skeletons, with ribs, gastralia and chevrons.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Complete shoulder and hip girdles, furculae, forelimbs with three-fingered clawed hands, hindlimbs and feet from numerous individuals.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Abundant healed injuries and infections, bone histology across a growth series and bite-marked prey bones; no skin, feathers, colour or gut contents are known.
